Weighted Distributions
A weighted distribution is one in which some options are more likely to come up than
others. Most of the examples that we've looked at so far involved linear distributions
of random possibilities, but it is a common desire as a designer to want to weight one
option more heavily than another. For example, in the board game Small World, the
designers wanted an attacker to get a random bonus on her final attack of each turn
about half of the time, and they wanted that bonus to range from +1 to +3. To do this,
they created a die with the six sides shown in Figure 11.11.
Figure 11.11 The attack bonus die from Small World with weighted bonus distribution
With this die, the chance of getting no bonus is 3/6 = 1/2 (0.5 = 50%), and the chance of
getting a bonus of 2 is 1/6 (0.1666 ≈ 17%), so the chance of no bonus is weighted much
more heavily than each of the other three choices.
What if instead, you still wanted the player to get a bonus only half of the time, but you
wanted for the bonus of 1 to be three times more likely than the 3, and the 2 to be twice
as likely as the 3? This would give us the weighted distribution shown in Figure 11.12.

Permutations
A traditional game called Bulls and Cows (see Figure 11.14) served as the basis for the
popular board game Master Mind (1970 by Mordecai Meirowitz). In this game, each
player starts by writing down a secret four-digit code (where each of the digits are

different). Players take turns trying to guess their opponent's code, and the first person
to guess correctly wins. When a player guesses, her opponent responds with a number
of bulls and a number of cows. The guesser gets a bull for each number she guessed
that is in the correct position and a cow for each number that is part of the code but not
in the right position. In Figure 11.14, black represents a bull, and white represents a cow.
Figure 11.14 An example game of Bulls and Cows
From the perspective of the guesser, the secret code is effectively a series of random
choices. Mathematicians call series like these permutations. In Bulls and Cows, the secret
code is a permutation of the ten digits 0–9, where four are chosen with no repeating
elements (i.e., the code can only contain one of each digit, making 1 40 1 illegal). In the
game Master Mind, there are eight possible colors, of which four are chosen with no rep-
etition. In both cases, the code is a permutation and not a combination because the posi-
tions of the elements matter (9305 is not the same as 3905). A combination is a selection
of choices where the position doesn't matter. For example, 1234, 2341, 3421, 2431, and
so on are all the same thing in a combination. A good example of a combination is the

Permutations with Repeating Elements
We'll start with permutations that allow repetition because the math is a little easier.
If there were four digits with repetition allowed, there would be 10,000 possible com-
binations (the numbers 0000 through 9999). This is easy to see with numbers, but we
need a more general way of thinking about it (for cases where there are not exactly
10 choices per slot). Because each digit is independent of the others and each has
10 possible choices, according to probability Rule 6, the probability of getting any
one number is 1/10 x 1/10 x 1/10 x 1/10 = 1/10,000. This also tells us that there are
10,000 possible choices for the code (if repetition is allowed).

The general calculation for permutations with repetition allowed is to multiply the
number of choices for each slot by each other. With four slots and ten choices each, this
is 10 x 10 x 10 x 10 = 10
4
= 10,000. If you were to make the code from six-sided dice
instead of digits, then there would be six choices per slot, making 6 x 6 x 6 x 6 = 6
4

1,296 possible choices.
Permutations with No Repeating Elements
But what about the actual case for Bulls and Cows where you're not allowed to repeat
any digits? It's actually simpler than you might imagine. After you've used a digit, it's no
longer available. So, for the first slot, you can pick any number from 0–9, but after a 9
has been chosen for the first slot, only 9 choices remain for the second slot (0–8). This
continues for the rest of the slots, so the calculation of possible codes for Bulls and Cows
is actually 10 x 9 x 8 x 7 = 5,040. Almost half of the possible choices are eliminated by
not allowing repeating digits.
Using Sheets to Balance Weapons
Another use of math and programs like Google Sheets in game design is the balance of
various weapons or abilities. In this section, we look at an example weapon balancing
process for a tactical combat board game similar to the video game Valkyria Chronicles
by Sega. In this example game, each weapon has three important values:
■ Shots: The number of shots fired at a time
■ D/Shot: The damage done by each shot
■ ToHit: The chance that each shot will hit at a given distance
As we balance these weapons, we want them to feel roughly equal to each other in
power, though we want each weapon to have a distinct personality. For each weapon,
these personalities are the following:
■ Pistol: A basic weapon; pretty decent in most situations but doesn't excel in any
■ Rifle: A good choice for mid and long range
■ Shotgun: Deadly up close but its power falls off quickly; only one shot, so a miss

Rebalancing the Weapons
Now that you have two sets of data and two charts, you can try rebalancing the weap-
ons. How will you make the machine gun more powerful? Will you increase its number
of shots, its chance to hit, or its damage per shot? There are some additional game rules
that we should keep in mind as we balance:
■ In this example game, units will have only 6 health, so they will fall unconscious if 6
or more damage is dealt to them.
■ In the example game, if an enemy is not downed by an attacking soldier, the enemy
will be allowed to counterattack. This makes dealing 6 damage in an attack much
more powerful than dealing 5 damage because it also protects the attacker from
counterattack.
■ Remember that weapons with many shots (e.g., the machine gun) will have a much
higher chance of dealing the average amount of damage in a single turn, whereas
guns with a single shot will feel much less reliable (e.g., the shotgun and sniper
rifle). Figure 11.7 shows how the probability distribution shifts toward the average
when you start rolling dice for multiple shots instead of a single one.

Even though this kind of spreadsheet-based balancing doesn't cover all possible implica-
tions of the design of the weapons, it's still a critical tool to have in your game design
arsenal because it can help you understand large amounts of data quickly. Several
designers of free-to-play games spend most of their day modifying spreadsheets to
make slight tweaks in game balance, so if you're interested in a job in that field, spread-
sheets and data-driven design (like you just did) are very important skills.
Positive and Negative Feedback
One final critical element of game balance to discuss are the concepts of positive
feedback and negative feedback. In a game with positive feedback, a player who takes an
early lead gains an advantage over the other players and is more likely to win the game.

In a game with negative feedback, the players who are losing have an advantage.
Poker is an excellent example of a game with positive feedback. If a player wins a big pot
and has more money than the other players, individual bets matter less to her, and she
has more freedom to do things like bluff (because she can afford to lose). However, a
player who loses early in the game and has little money left can't afford to take risks and
has less freedom when playing. Monopoly has a strong positive feedback mechanism
where the player with the best properties consistently gets more money and is able to
force other players to sell their properties to her if they can't afford the rent when they
land on her spaces. Positive feedback is generally frowned upon in most games, but it
can be very good if you want the game to end quickly (though Monopoly does not take
advantage of this; for info on why this may be, check out Chapter 8, "Design Goals").
Single-player games also often have positive feedback mechanisms to make the player
feel increasingly powerful throughout the game.
Mario Kart is a great example of a game with negative feedback in the form of the
random items that it awards to players when they drive through item boxes. The player
in the lead will usually only get a banana (a largely defensive weapon), a set of three

bananas, or a green shell (one of the weakest attacks). A player in last place will often
get much more powerful items like the lightning bolt that will slow down every other
player in the race or the dreaded blue shell. Negative feedback makes games feel fairer
to the players who are not in the lead and generally leads to both longer games and
to all players feeling that they still have a chance of winning even if they're pretty far
behind.
Summary
This chapter covered a lot of math, but I hope you saw that learning a little about math
will be useful for you as a game designer. Most of the topics covered in this chapter
could merit their own book or course, so I encourage you to look into them further if
your interest has been piqued.

GUIDING THE PLAYER
As you've read in earlier chapters, your primary
job as a designer is to craft an experience for
players to enjoy. However, the further you get
into your project and your design, the more
obvious and intuitive your game appears to
you. This comes from your familiarity with the
game and is entirely natural.
However, this means that you need to keep
a wary eye on your game, making sure that
players who have never seen your game before
also intuitively understand what they need to
do to experience the game as you intended.
This requires careful, sometimes invisible,
guidance, and it is the topic of this chapter.
Humble Bundle Pearson Game Design and Development Bundle — © Pearson. Do Not Distribute.
232 CHAPTER 12 GUIdInG the Player
This chapter covers two styles of player guidance: direct, where the player knows that
they are being guided; and indirect, where the guidance is so subtle that players often
don't even realize that the guidance is there. The chapter concludes with information
about sequencing, a style of progressive instruction useful in teaching players new con-
cepts or introducing them to new game mechanics.
Direct Guidance
Direct guidance methods are those that the player is explicitly aware of. Direct guidance
takes many forms, but in all of them, quality is determined by immediacy, scarcity, brev-
ity, and clarity:
■ Immediacy: The message must be given to the player when it is immediately
relevant. Some games try to tell the player all the various controls for the game at
the very beginning (sometimes showing a diagram of the controller with all the but-
tons labeled), but it is ridiculous to think that a player will be able to remember all
of these controls when the time comes that they actually need to use them. Direct
information about controls should be provided immediately the first time that the
player needs it. In the PlayStation 2 game Kya: Dark Lineage, a tree falls into the path
of the player character that they must jump over, and as it is falling, the game shows
the player the message "Press X to jump" at exactly the time they need to know that
information.
1
The 2021 Nintendo Switch game Metroid Dread has an interesting example of im-
mediacy. Throughout the game, the main character Samus occasionally gains the
Omega Cannon ability, which has different controls than her regular weapons. To
make sure that the player remembers how to use these unique weapon controls, the
game requires the player to use the Omega Cannon properly to exit the room when-
ever they obtain it. This gives the player a chance to practice the unique controls in
a non-threatening situation, immediately before they use them to defeat a terrifying
boss that is hunting Samus.
2
■ Scarcity: Many modern games have lots of controls and lots of simultaneous goals.

It is important that the player not be flooded with too much information all at one
time. Making instructions and other direct controls scarcer makes them more valu-
able to the player and more likely to be heeded. This is also the case with missions.
A player can only really concentrate on a single mission at once. This is a common
issue in many fantastic open world games like Skyrim, which inundate the player

Honestly, Kya: Dark Lineage is still the best example I've ever seen of presenting a ton of game

2. This is also an example of the isolated introduction described in the "Sequencing" section near
the end of this chapter.

with various missions to the point that after several hours of gameplay, they could
potentially be in the middle of dozens of different missions, many of which will never
be completed.
■ Brevity: Never use more verbiage than is necessary, and don't give the player too
much information at one time. In the tactical combat game Valkyria Chronicles, if you
wanted to teach the player to press O to take cover behind some sandbags, the least
you would need to say is, "When near sandbags, press O to take cover and reduce
damage from enemy attacks."
■ Clarity: Be very clear about what you're trying to convey. In the previous example,
you might be tempted to just tell the player, "When standing near sandbags, press O
to take cover," because you might assume that players should know that cover will
shield them from incoming bullets. However, in Valkyria Chronicles, cover not only
shields you but also drastically reduces the amount of damage you take from bullets
that do hit (even if the cover is not between the attacker and the target). For the
player to understand everything they need to know about cover, they must also be
told about the damage reduction.
Methods of Direct Guidance
There are a number of methods of direct guidance:
■ Instructions: The game explicitly tells the player what to do. These can take the
form of text, dialogue with an authoritative non-player character (NPC), or visual dia-
grams and often incorporate combinations of the three. Instructions are one of the
clearest forms of direct guidance, but they also have the greatest likelihood of either
overwhelming the player with too much information or annoying them by pedanti-
cally telling them information they already know.
■ Call to action: The game explicitly gives the player an action to perform and a
reason to do so. This often takes the form of missions that are given to the player by

NPCs. A good strategy is to present the player with a clear long-term goal and then
give them progressively smaller medium- and short-term goals that must be accom-
plished on the way to the long-term goal.
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time begins with the fairy Navi waking Link to tell
him that he has been summoned by the Great Deku Tree. This is then reinforced by
the first person Link encounters upon leaving his home, who tells him that it is a
great honor to be summoned by the tree and that he should hurry. This gives Link
a clear long-term goal of seeking the Great Deku Tree (and the Great Deku Tree's
conversation with Navi before Link is awoken hints to the player that Link will be as-
signed a much longer-term goal when he arrives). Link's path to the Great Deku Tree
is blocked by Mido, who tells him that he will need a sword and shield before ventur-
ing into the forest. This gives the player two medium-term goals that are required
before they can achieve their long-term goal. Along the way to obtaining both, Link

must navigate a small maze, converse with several people, and earn at least 40 ru-
pees. These are all short-term, clear goals that are directly tied to the long-term goal
of reaching the Great Deku Tree.
■ Map or guidance system: Many games include a map or other GPS-style guid-
ance system that directs the player toward their goals or toward the next step in their
mission. For example, Grand Theft Auto V has a radar/mini-map in the corner of the
screen with a highlighted route for the player to follow to the next objective. The
world of GTA V is so vast that missions will often take the player into an unfamiliar
part of the map, where the player relies very heavily on the GPS. However, be aware
that this kind of guidance can lead to players spending most of their time just follow-
ing the directions of the virtual GPS rather than actually thinking about a destination
and choosing a path of their own, which can increase the time it takes for the player
to learn the layout of the game world.
■ Pop-ups: Some games have contextual controls that change based on the objects
near the player. In Assassin's Creed IV: Black Flag, the same button controls such
diverse actions as opening doors, lighting barrels of gunpowder on fire, and taking
control of mounted weapons. To help the player understand all these possibilities,
pop-ups with the icon for the button and a very short description of the action ap-
pear whenever an action is possible. This method also includes the short videos that
show your character performing a special move to help you decide whether or not to
purchase it when leveling up, as seen in God of War (2018) and Star Wars Jedi: Fallen

Indirect Guidance
Indirect guidance is the art of influencing and guiding the player without them actually
knowing that they are being controlled. Several different methods of indirect guidance
can be useful to you as a designer. I was first introduced to the idea of indirect guidance by
Jesse Schell, who presents it as "indirect control" in Chapter 16 of his book, The Art of Game
Design: A Book of Lenses. This list is an expansion of his six methods of indirect control.
3
Constraints
If you give the player limited choices, they will choose one of them. This seems elemen-
tary, but think about the difference between a question that asks you to fill in the blank
and one that gives you four choices to pick from. Without constraint, players run the
risk of choice paralysis, which occurs when a person is presented with so many choices
that they can't effectively weigh them all against each other and are therefore unable to
make a choice. This is the same reason that a restaurant menu might have 100 different
3. Jesse Schell, The Art of Game Design: A Book of Lenses (Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, 2008),
283–298.
Humble Bundle Pearson Game Design and Development Bundle — © Pearson. Do Not Distribute.

items on it but only feature images of 20. The restaurant owners want to make it easier
for you to make a decision about dinner.
Goals
In the previous section of this chapter, we discussed ways that you can use multiple lev-
els of goals for direct guidance. Goals can also be used to guide the player indirectly. As
Schell points out, if the player has a goal to collect bananas and has two possible doors
to go through, placing clearly visible bananas behind one of the doors will encourage
the player to head toward the door with bananas.
Players are also often willing to create their own goals, to which you can guide them by
giving them the materials to achieve those goals. In the game Minecraft (the name of
which includes the two direct instructions: "mine" and "craft"), the designers defined
the materials required to craft various items, and these design choices in turn imply the
goals that players are able to create for themselves. Because most of the simplest recipes
allow the player to make building materials, simple tools, and weapons, these recipes
start the player down the path toward building a defensible fort to make their home.
That goal then causes the player to explore for materials. For example, the knowledge
that diamond makes the best tools will lead a player to explore deeper and deeper tun-
nels to find diamond (which is rare and only occurs at depths of about 50–55 meters)
and encourage them to expand the amount of the world that they have seen.
Physical Interface
Schell's book covers information about how the shape of a physical interface can be

used to indirectly guide the player: If you give a player of Guitar Hero or Rock Band a
guitar-shaped controller, they will generally expect to use it to play music. Giving a
Guitar Hero player a regular game controller might lead them to think that they could
control their character's movement around the stage (because a standard game control-
ler usually directs character movement), but with a guitar, the player's thoughts focus
on making music.
Another way in which the sense of touch can be used for indirect guidance is through
the rumble feature on many game controllers, which enables the controller to vibrate
in the player's hands at various intensities. Actual automobile racetracks include red
and white rumble strips on the inside of turns. The rumble strips alternate height along
with color, allowing the driver to feel rumbling in the steering wheel if their wheel goes
too far to the inside of the turn and makes contact with the rumble strip. This is helpful
because racers are often trying to be as close to the inside of a turn as possible to be on
the perfect racing line, and it's not possible to see exactly where the wheels are touch-
ing the road from inside the car. This same method is used in many racing games, rum-
bling the controller when the player is at the extreme inside edge of a turn. Expanding

on this, you could imagine keeping the controller still when the player is on the track
but causing it to rumble erratically if the player goes off the track into some grass. The
tactile sensation would help the player understand that they should return to the track.
Visual Design
You can use visuals in several different ways to indirectly guide the player:
■ Light: Humans are naturally drawn to light. If you place a player in a dark room with
a pool of light at one end, they will usually move toward that light before exploring
anything else.
■ Similarity: When a player has seen that something in the world is good in some
way (helpful, healing, valuable, etc.), they will seek out similar things.
■ Trails: Similarity can lead to a breadcrumb-trail-like effect where the player picks up
a certain item and then follows a trail of similar items to a location that the designer
wants them to explore.
■ Landmarks: Visually interesting and distinct objects can be used as landmarks.
At the beginning of Journey by thatgamecompany, the player starts in the middle
of a desert next to a sand dune. Everything around them looks like sand and dunes
except for a few dark stone markers atop the tallest nearby dune (see Figure 12.1,
image A). Because this group of markers is the only thing in the landscape that
stands out, the player is driven to move up the dune toward it. As the player reaches

bursting from the top (see Figure 12.1, image B). The camera move causes the
mountain to emerge from directly behind the stone markers, signifying to the player
that the mountain is their new goal. The camera move directly transfers the goal
state from the markers to the mountain.

When initially designing Disneyland, Walt Disney Imagineering (which at the time
was named WED Enterprises) designed various landmarks to guide guests around
the park and keep them from bunching up in the main hub. When guests first enter
the park, they are located in Main Street USA, which looks like an idealized small

American town from the early twentieth century. However, very soon into their jour-
ney down Main Street, they notice Sleeping Beauty's Castle at the end of the street
and are immediately drawn to it. Upon finally reaching the castle, guests notice
that it is much smaller than it initially appeared and that there's really nothing to
do there. Now that they are in the main hub of Disneyland, they can see the moun-
tain of the Matterhorn rising in front of them, the space-age statue at the entrance
to Tomorrowland to their right, and the fort of Frontierland to their left. From their
position in the hub, these new landmarks look much more interesting than the small
castle, and guests soon leave the castle area to disperse through the park toward
these new landmarks.

Landmarks are also used throughout the Assassin's Creed series. Whenever a player
first enters a new part of the map, they see that there are a few structures that are
taller than the others in the area. In addition to the natural attraction of these land-
marks, each is also a viewpoint in the game from which the player can synchronize,
a process that updates their in-game map with detailed information about the area.
Because the designers have given the player both a landmark and a goal (filling in
the map), they can guess that players will often seek a viewpoint as their first activity
in a new part of the world.

ages, the player (as Drake) is chasing an enemy named Talbot.

■ Contrast: The shots in Figures 12.2 and 12.3 each also demonstrate the use of
contrast to guide player attention. There are several forms of contrast demonstrated
in Figures 12.2 and 12.3 that contribute to player guidance:
■ Brightness: In shots A and B of Figure 12.2, the ledge and the wall that form
arrows have the highest range of brightness contrast in the image. The dark areas
alongside light areas cause the lines to stand out visually.
■ Texture: In shots A and B of Figure 12.2, the wooden planks are smooth while
the surrounding stone textures are rough. In shots C and D of Figure 12.2, the
soft texture of the blue fabric contrasts with the hard stone on which it rests. By
laying over the stone edge, the fabric also serves to soften the edge, making the
player more aware that they can leap over it.
■ Color: In shots C and D of Figure 12.2, the blue fabric, yellow window frame,
and yellow bars contrast with the other colors (or lack thereof) in the scene. In
shot D of Figure 12.3, the yellow rung at the bottom stands out because the rest

■ Directionality: Though it is not as commonly used as the other three, contrast in
directionality can also be used effectively to draw the eye. In shot A of Figure 12.3,

Audio Design
Schell states that music can influence the player's mood and thereby their behavior.
5
Certain types of music have become linked to various types of activity: Slow, quiet,
somewhat jazzy music is often linked to activities like sneaking or searching for clues (as
seen in the Scooby Doo cartoon series), whereas loud, fast, powerful music (like that in
an action movie) is better suited to scenes where the player is expected to brazenly fight
through enemies and feel invincible.
Sound effects can also be used to influence player behavior by drawing attention to
possible actions that the player can take. In the Assassin's Creed series, a shimmering,
ringing sound effect plays whenever the player is near a treasure chest. This informs the
player that they could choose to take the action of looking for the chest and, because it
only happens when a chest is nearby, it tells them that it wouldn't be too far out of the
way to do so. With a guaranteed reward in close proximity, the player is usually guided
to search for the chest unless they are already engaged in another more important
activity.
Player Avatar
The model of the player's avatar (i.e., player character) can have a strong effect on
player behavior. If the player character looks like a rock star and is holding a guitar, the

player might expect for their character to be able to play music. If the player character
has a sword, the player would expect to be able to hit things and run into combat. If
the player character walks around in a wizard hat and long robe while holding a book
instead of a weapon, the player would be encouraged to stay back from direct combat
and focus on spells.
Non-Player Characters
Non-player characters (NPCs) in games are one of the most complex and flexible forms
of indirect player guidance, and that guidance can take many forms.
Modeling Behavior
NPC characters can model several different types of behavior. In games, behavior model-
ing is the act of demonstrating a specific behavior and allowing the player to see the
consequences of that behavior. Figure 12.4 shows various examples of behavior model-
ing in the game Kya: Dark Lineage by Atari. Types of modeling include
■ Negative behavior: In modeling negative behavior, the NPC does something that
the player should avoid doing and demonstrates the consequences. In image A of

Another way in which NPCs influence player behavior is through the emotional connec-
tions that the player develops with them.

It is also possible to cause the player to follow an NPC because of a negative emotional
connection. For example, the NPC could steal something from the player and run, caus-
ing the player to chase him to retrieve their property. In either case, the reaction of the
player is almost always to follow the NPC, making this a very strong form of indirect
control.
Teaching New Skills and Concepts
Although direct and indirect guidance usually focus on moving the player through the
virtual locations of the game, this final section is devoted to guiding the player to a bet-
ter understanding of how to play the game.
In simple games with very few controls, it is possible to present the player with a dia-
gram of the controls or even to just let them experiment. In Super Mario Bros. (1985) for
the Nintendo Entertainment System (NES), one button caused Mario to jump, and the
other button caused him to run (and to shoot fireballs, after he picked up a fire flower).
Through just a small amount of experimentation, the player could easily understand the
functions of the A and B buttons on the NES controller. Modern controllers, however,
typically have two analog sticks (that can also be clicked like buttons), one 8-direction
D-Pad, six face buttons, two shoulder buttons, and two triggers. Even with all of these
possible controls, many modern games have so many possible interactions allowed to

current context (as was mentioned when discussing pop-ups in the direct guidance

With so much complexity in some modern games, it becomes critical to teach the player
how to play the game as they go along. An instruction booklet won't cut it anymore;
now the player needs to be guided though experiences that are properly sequenced.
Sequencing
Sequencing is the art of gently presenting new information to the player, and most
examples follow the basic style shown in Figure 12.6. The figure shows several steps

player would receive the lightning spell in a room with locked doors and must use the

using the spell in combat but also demonstrates how powerful the spell is, making the
player feel powerful as well.
Integration
After the player understands how to use the new game mechanic in isolation (as
described in the previous examples), it's time to teach them how to combine it with
other mechanics. This can be done explicitly (e.g., the player could be told that cast-
ing the lightning spell in water will expand its range from a 6-foot radius when used
outside the water to the entire pool of water when used in the water) or implicitly (e.g.,
the player could be placed in combat in a pool of water with enemies approaching, and
they would notice that when they used the lightning spell, everything in the water was
electrocuted, not just those enemies within 6 feet). Later in the game, when the player
learns a spell that allows them to drench their enemies and cause a temporary pool of
water, they will immediately realize that this also allows them to expand the reach of
their lightning spell.
Summary
There are many more methods of player guidance than could fit in this chapter, but
I hope that it gave you a good introduction not only to some specific methods but
also the reasoning behind why those methods are used. As you design your games,
remember to keep player guidance in mind at all times. This can be one of the toughest
things to do because to you, as the designer, every game mechanic will seem obvious.
Breaking out of your own perspective is so difficult that most game companies will seek
dozens or hundreds of one-time testers to play their game throughout the development
process. It is critically important as a designer to always find new people to test your
game and give you feedback on the quality of the guidance from the perspective of
someone who has never seen the game before. Games developed in isolation without
the benefit of naïve testers will often either be too difficult for new players or at least
have uneven, staggered rises in difficulty that cause frustration. As described in

PUZZLE DESIGN
Puzzles are an important part of many
digital games as well as an interesting design
challenge in their own right. This chapter starts
by exploring puzzle design through the eyes
of one of the greatest living puzzle designers,
Scott Kim.
The latter part of the chapter explores various
types of puzzles that are common in modern
games, some of which might not be what you
would expect.
Humble Bundle Pearson Game Design and Development Bundle — © Pearson. Do Not Distribute.
248 CHAPTER 13 PUzzle desIGn
As you'll learn through this chapter, most single-player games have some sort of puzzle
in them, though multiplayer games often do not. The primary reason for this is that
both single-player games and puzzles rely on the game system to provide challenge
to the player, whereas multiplayer digital games (that are not cooperative) more often
rely on other human players to provide the challenge. Because of this parallel between
single-player games and puzzles, learning about how to design puzzles can help you
with the design of any game in which you intend to have a single-player or cooperative
mode.
Scott Kim on Puzzle Design
Scott Kim is one of today's leading puzzle designers. Since 1990, he has written puzzles
for magazines such as Discover, Scientific American, and Games, and he has designed the
puzzle modes of several games including Bejeweled 2. He has lectured about puzzle
design at both the TED conference and the Game Developers Conference. His influen-
tial full-day workshop, "The Art of Puzzle Design"
1
—which he delivered with Alexey
Pajitnov (the creator of Tetris) at the 1999 and 2000 Game Developers Conferences—has
shaped many game designers' ideas about puzzles for the last two decades. This chap-
ter explores some of the content of that workshop. Throughout this chapter, I mostly
discuss the concepts of puzzle design presented in that workshop, but I also add more
aspects and examples that have emerged over the subsequent two decades.
Defining Puzzle
Kim states that his favorite definition of puzzle is also one of the simplest:
"A puzzle is fun, and it has a right answer." 2
This differentiates puzzles from toys, which are fun but don't have a right answer, and
from games, which are fun but have a goal rather than a specific correct answer. Kim
sees puzzles as separate from games, although I personally see them as more of a highly
developed subset of games. Even though this definition of puzzles is very simple, some
important subtleties lie hidden within.

Game Developers Conference, San Jose, CA, March 15, 1999). Accessed June 30, 2021.

GDC99/gdc1999.ppt
2. Scott Kim, "What Is a Puzzle?" Accessed June 30, 2021. https://web.archive.org/

A Puzzle Is Fun
Kim states that puzzles have three elements of fun:
2
■ Novelty: Many puzzles rely on a certain specific insight to solve them, and after the
player has gained that insight, finding the puzzle's solution is rather simple. A large
part of the fun of solving a puzzle is that flash of insight, the joy we feel when we've
created a new solution. If a puzzle lacks novelty, the player will often already have
the insight required to solve it before even starting the puzzle, and thus that element
of the puzzle's fun is lost.
■ Appropriate difficulty: Just as games must seek to give the player an adequate
challenge, puzzles must also be matched to the player's skill, experience, and type
of creativity. Each player approaching a puzzle has a unique level of experience
with puzzles of that type and a certain level of frustration that they are willing to
experience before giving up. Some of the best puzzles in this regard have both an
adequate solution that is of medium difficulty and an expert solution that requires
advanced skill to discover. Another great strategy for puzzle design is to create a
puzzle that appears to be simple although it is actually quite difficult. If the player
perceives the puzzle to be simple, they'll be less likely to give up.
■ Trickiness: Many great puzzles cause the player to shift their perspective or thinking
to solve them. However, even after having that perspective shift, the player should
still feel that executing their plan to solve the puzzle requires skill and cunning. One
excellent example of this is the puzzle-based stealth combat of Klei Entertainment's
Mark of the Ninja, in which the player must use insight to solve the puzzle of how to
approach a room full of enemies and then—after they have a plan—must physically
execute that plan with precision.
It Has a Right Answer
Every puzzle needs to have a right answer, although many puzzles have several right
answers. One of the key elements of a great puzzle is that after the player has found the
right answer, it is clearly obvious to them that they are right. If the correctness of the
answer isn't easily evident, the puzzle can seem muddled and unsatisfying.
It's Also "Puzzling"
When we say that we find something "puzzling" there is a lot of meaning loaded
into that term that designers should keep in mind.
3
Puzzling means that we lack the

from "confusing," which would also mean that we lacked the solution but that we either
didn't care to know it or that we didn't have any hope of finding it on our own.
Genres of Puzzles
Kim identifies four genres of puzzle (see Figure 13.1), each of which causes the player to
take a different approach and use different skills. These genres are at the point of inter-
section between puzzles and other activities. For example, a story puzzle is the mixture
of a narrative and a series of puzzles.
Figure 13.1 Kim's four genres of puzzles 4
■ Action: Action puzzles like Tetris have time pressure and allow players a chance
to fix their mistakes. They are the combination of an action game with a puzzle
mindset. This also includes rhythm games (e.g., PaRappa the Rapper and Rock Band)
and what I call twitch puzzle games (e.g., Oddworld: Abe's Oddysee or boss battles
in Metroid Dread, where the player must solve the puzzle of which inputs they must
enter at exactly the right time to succeed).
4. Adapted from Scott Kim and Alexey Pajitnov, "The Art of Puzzle Game Design," slide 7.
Humble Bundle Pearson Game Design and Development Bundle — © Pearson. Do Not Distribute.

■ Story: Story puzzles like Myst, the Professor Layton series, and most hidden-object
games have puzzles that players must solve to progress through the plot and explore
the environment. They combine narrative and puzzles.
5
■ Construction: Construction games invite the player to build an object from parts
to solve a certain problem. One of the most successful of these was The Incredible
Machine, in which players built Rube Goldberg–like contraptions to cause the cats
in each scene to run away. The construction game Fantastic Contraption began as
a Flash-based web game in 2008 and was redeveloped into a launch title that was
bundled with the HTC Vive virtual reality headset. Some construction games even in-
clude a construction set that allows the player to design and distribute puzzles. They
are the intersection of construction, engineering, and spatial reasoning with puzzles.
■ Strategy: Many of what Kim calls strategy puzzle games are the solitaire versions
of the kinds of puzzles that players encounter in games that are traditionally multi-
player. These include things like bridge puzzles (which present players with various
hands in a bridge game and ask how play should proceed) and chess puzzles (which
give players a few chess pieces positioned on a board and ask how the player could
achieve checkmate in a certain number of moves). These combine the thinking
required for the multiplayer version of the game with the skill building of a puzzle to

■ Pure puzzles: Kim also holds that some pure puzzles don't fit in any of the other
four genres. These include games like Sudoku or crossword puzzles and would sit in
the middle of Figure 13.1 rather than in any of the other four genres.
The Four Major Reasons that People Play
Puzzles
Kim's research and experience have led him to believe that people primarily play
puzzles for the following reasons:
6
■ Challenge: People like to feel challenged and to feel the joy of overcoming those
challenges. Puzzles are an easy way for players to feel a sense of achievement,
accomplishment, and progress.
5. Myst was one of the first CD-ROM adventure games, and was the number one best-selling
CD-ROM game until The Sims took that title. The Professor Layton series of games comprises
many titles for Nintendo's handheld platforms (and now Android and iOS as well) that each
wrap many individual puzzles inside an overarching mystery story. Hidden-object games are
a popular genre of game where a player must find a list of hidden objects in a complicated
scene. These games often have mystery plots that the player is attempting to solve by finding
the objects.
6. Scott Kim and Alexey Pajitnov, "The Art of Puzzle Game Design," slide 8.

■ ■ Mindless distraction: Some people seek big challenges, but others are more
interested in having something interesting to do to pass the time. Several puzzles like
Bejeweled and Angry Birds don't provide the player with a big challenge but rather
a low-stress interesting distraction. Puzzle games of this type should be relatively
simple and repetitive rather than relying on a specific insight (requiring a specific
insight is more common in puzzles played for challenge).
■ ■ Character and environment: People like great stories and characters, beautiful
images, and interesting environments. Story puzzles such as Myst, The Journeyman
Project, the Professor Layton series, and The Room series rely on their stories and art to
propel the player through the game.
■ ■ Spiritual journey: Finally, some puzzles mimic spiritual journeys in a couple of
different ways. Some famous puzzles such as Rubik's Cube can be seen as a rite of
passage—either you've solved one in your life, or you haven't. Many mazes work on
this same principle. Additionally, puzzles can mimic the archetypical hero's journey:
The player starts in regular life, encounters a puzzle that sends them into a realm of
struggle, fights against the puzzle for a while, gains an epiphany of insight, and then
can easily defeat the puzzle that had stymied them just moments earlier.
Modes of Thought Required by Puzzles

Single-Mode Puzzle Types
The following list describes the single-mode puzzle types shown in Figure 13.2:
■ Word: There are many different kinds of word puzzles, most of which rely on the
player having a large and varied vocabulary. Word puzzles are often particularly
good if you're designing games for older adults, because most people's vocabularies
peak later in life.
8
■ Image & Media: Kim and Pajitnov called these Image puzzles, which included
jigsaw, hidden-object, and 2D/3D spatial puzzles. Image puzzles tend to exercise the
parts of the brain connected to visual/spatial processing and pattern recognition.
However, there are now also examples of puzzles that use other types of media and
engage the parts of the brain that recognize them; for example, an audio puzzle
that involves rhythm or music. The puzzles that players encounter when interpreting
truth or lies in the police interrogations of L.A. Confidential use video and body lan-
guage, whereas the moments frozen in time in the 2018 mystery game Return of the
Obra Din require the player to carefully explore and understand spatial and temporal
information.
9
■ Logic: Logic puzzles such as Bulls and Cows (described in Chapter 11, "Math and
Game Balance"), riddles, and deduction puzzles cause players to exercise their
logical reasoning. Many games are based on deductive reasoning: the top-down
elimination of several false possibilities, leaving only one possibility that must be true
(e.g., a player reasoning, "I know that all the other suspects are innocent, so Colonel
Mustard must have killed Mr. Boddy"). These include Clue, Bulls and Cows, and logic
grid puzzles. Far fewer games use inductive reasoning: the bottom-up extrapolation
from a specific certainty to a general probability (e.g., a player reasoning, "The last
five times that John bluffed in poker, he habitually scratched his nose; John is scratch-
ing his nose now, so he's probably bluffing"). Deductive logic leads to certainty,
whereas inductive logic makes an educated guess based on reasonable probability.
The certainty of the answers has traditionally made deductive logic more attractive

■ Word / Image: Many games, such as Scrabble, rebuses (like the one in Figure 13.3),
and word searches, incorporate both the word and image modes of thought to
solve. Scrabble is a mixed-mode puzzle, but crossword puzzles are not, because
in Scrabble the player is determining where to place the word and attempting to

require either of these two acts of visual/spatial reasoning and decision-making.
■ Image / Logic: Sliding block puzzles, laser mazes, and puzzles like those shown in

Kim's Eight Steps of Digital Puzzle Design
Scott Kim describes eight steps that he typically goes through when designing a
puzzle:
10
1. Inspiration: Just like a game, inspiration for a puzzle can come from anywhere.
Alexey Pajitnov has stated that his inspiration for Tetris was the mathematician
Solomon Golomb's concept of pentominoes (12 different shapes, each made of
five blocks, which could be fit together into an optimal space-filling puzzle) and the
desire to use them in an action game. However, there were too many different five-
block pentomino shapes, so he reduced it to the seven different four-block tetromi-
noes found in Tetris.
2. Simplification: Usually, you need to go through some form of simplification to get
from your original inspiration to a playable puzzle.
a. Identify the core puzzle mechanic: the essential tricky skill required.
b. Eliminate any irrelevant details and narrow the focus.
c. Make pieces uniform. For example, if you're dealing with a construction
puzzle, move the pieces onto a uniform grid to make it easier for the player to
manipulate.
d. Simplify the controls. Make sure that the controls for the puzzle are appropri-
ate to the interface. Kim talks about how great a Rubik's Cube feels in real life
but how terrible it would be to manipulate a digital version with a mouse and
keyboard.
3. Construction set: Build a tool that makes construction of puzzles quick and easy.
Many puzzles can be built and tested as paper prototypes, but if that isn't the case
for your puzzle, this is the first place that you will need to do some programming.
Regardless of whether it is paper or digital, an effective construction set can make
the creation of additional levels much easier for you. Discover which tasks are repeti-
tive time-wasters in the puzzle construction process and see whether you can make
reusable parts or automated processes for them.
4. Rules: Define and clarify the rules. This includes defining the board, the pieces, the
ways that they can move, and the ultimate goal of the puzzle or level.
5. Make Several Levels: Create examples of the puzzle. Make sure that you design
different levels of difficulty that explore various elements of your design and game
mechanics.
6. Testing: Just like a game, you don't know how players will react to a puzzle until
you place it in front of them. Even with his many years of experience, Kim still finds

Usually, step 6 leads the designer to iteratively return to steps 4 and 5 and refine
previous decisions. Because of the importance of insight in so many puzzles, you
may need to find new playtesters for each iteration (this is less the case for puzzles
like Tetris, which are replayable because they don't rely on a specific insight to solve
them).
7. Sequence: After you have refined the rules of the puzzle and have several levels
designed, it's time to put them in a meaningful sequence. Each new concept should
be introduced in isolation, only requiring the player to use that single concept in the
most elementary way. You can then progressively increase the difficulty of the puzzle
that must be solved using that concept. Finally, you can create puzzles that mix that
concept with other concepts that the player already understands. This advice from
Kim is very similar to the sequencing in Chapter 12, "Guiding the Player," that most
experts recommend for teaching any new game concept to a player. An excellent
example of this is the puzzle game Scalak,

which sequences the introduction of
several game mechanics without any text at all.
8. Presentation: With the levels, rules, and sequence all created, it's now time to
refine the look of the puzzle. Presentation also includes refinements to the interface
and to the way you display that information to the player. Of course, if it's something
like a riddle or an audio puzzle, this is where you would spend time refining those
aspects of presentation as well.
Seven Goals of Effective Puzzle Design
You need to keep several things in mind when designing a puzzle. Generally, the more
of these goals that you can meet, the better puzzle you will create:
■ User friendly: Puzzles should be familiar and rewarding to their players. Puzzles
can rely on tricks, but they should not take advantage of the player or make the
player feel stupid.
■ Ease of entry: Within one minute, the player must understand how to play the
puzzle. Within a few minutes, the player should be immersed in the experience.
■ Instant feedback: The puzzle should be "juicy" in the way that Kyle Gabler
(co-creator of World of Goo and Little Inferno) uses the word: The puzzle should
actively react to player input in a way that feels physical, active, and energetic.
■ Perpetual motion: The puzzle should constantly prod the player to take the next
step, and there should be no clear stopping point. When I worked at Pogo.com, all

■ Crystal-clear goals: The player should always clearly understand the primary goal
of the puzzle. However, having advanced goals for players to discover over time is
also useful. The puzzle games Hexic and Bookworm are examples of puzzles that have
very clear initial goals and also include advanced expert goals that veteran players
can discover and enjoy over time.
■ Difficulty levels: The player should be able to engage the puzzle at a level
of difficulty that is appropriate to their skill. As with all games, appropriate puzzle
difficulty is critical to making the experience fun for players.
■ Something special: Most great puzzle games include something that makes them
unique and interesting. Alexey Pajitnov's game Tetris combines apparent simplicity
with the chance for deep strategy and steadily increasing intensity. Both World of Goo
and Angry Birds have incredibly juicy, reactive gameplay.
The Steps of Solving a Puzzle
Though Kim and Pajitnov explored many aspects of designing puzzles, they did not talk
much about the process a puzzler (i.e., player of a puzzle) goes through when solving a
puzzle. It's important to keep these steps in mind as you're designing puzzles, especially
because it can help you understand where you might be losing people who give up on
your puzzle. In some cases, not all of these steps will occur, but the steps that a puzzler
can go through to solve a puzzler include:
1. Understanding the goal: The puzzler knows what they are trying to accomplish.
2. Exploration: The puzzler tries several different things to see if one of them works.
3. Insight: The puzzler gets a flash of inspiration/understanding that might be the
solution to the puzzle.
4. Attempt: The puzzler tests their insight to see if it was correct. In many puzzles, this
phase is very short (e.g., the puzzler gets any idea for a word in a crossword puzzle
and then checks to see whether it fits). In other cases—particularly in the case of
action puzzles—the puzzler may know exactly what they need to do, yet it could still
take several attempts before they accomplish it.
5. Mastery: The puzzler correctly performs the solution of the puzzle.
We'll explore each step in turn.
Understanding the Goal
If the goal of your puzzle isn't clear, puzzlers often won't even start. Within the first
few minutes of Return of the Obra Din, you are given the goal: "Use the pocketwatch

Exploration
After the player knows the goal, they begin exploring the space of the puzzle. This
includes everything from exploration of the physical space of an escape room to
exploration of game mechanics such as rules, point systems, or even physics simula-
tions. The more a puzzler learns about the space of the puzzle, the closer they are to
an insight.
It's worth noting that some puzzle games go back and forth between understanding
the goal and exploration, allowing the player to discover a deeper understanding of
their goal as they play. This is particularly true of point-and-click adventure games, but
could be said to be true of any puzzle game where more goals are revealed through
play.
12
Insight
At some point—usually in a flash—the puzzler gains the insight that will enable them to
solve the puzzle. For some puzzles, this insight comes with certainty, and the puzzler
also knows at this point that they are correct. Other times, this is just a vague intuition
that the solution lies in a specific direction or the realization that maybe something that
was assumed to be a rule or boundary of the puzzle isn't actually a requirement for the
puzzle (both of the Image/Logic puzzle examples in this chapter require the puzzler to
break assumptions to solve them).
Attempt
In some cases, after the puzzler has gained insight, they can solve the puzzle imme-
diately, achieving mastery on their first attempt. In other cases, it may take several
attempts for one of several reasons:
■ If their insight was incorrect or incomplete, then the puzzler will attempt to solve the
puzzle and fail, returning them to the exploration phase.
■ If the insight was not yet specific enough—for example, if the player of an action-
adventure game does something that significantly damages a boss, but they aren't

This last bullet happens with many boss enemies in games such as Demon Souls, where
the player knows what to do but there is still a large gap between their intent to per-
form an action (like dodging a boss enemy's sequence of attacks) and actually correctly
tapping the buttons on the controller at exactly the right moment to succeed. In his
2013 talk at the Game Developers Conference, Nels Anderson, the lead designer of Mark
of the Ninja, spoke about narrowing this gulf between intent and execution.

In Mark
of the Ninja, the player is able to freeze time at any moment, allowing them time to plan
and make precision movements. The team found that doing this made it significantly
easier for a player to execute their plans in the game, which shifted the skill of the game
from physical execution (requiring many attempts) to mental planning, making the
game more puzzle-like and more interesting to players.
Mastery
The puzzle is solved. For puzzles that only require one or two attempts, the moment of
mastery isn't very significant. For other puzzles, especially those that require dexterity
or timing, mastery can be a huge moment. This is especially true of finally winning a
boss battle in a difficult action game like Guacamelee. In typical "Metroidvania"

style,
Guacamelee 's boss battles rely on the player learning the boss's attack patterns and
solving the dexterity and timing puzzle of how to avoid damage and find moments to
counterattack. Then, after gaining the insight into each attack and how to avoid it, the
player often must attempt the fight multiple times before succeeding at defeating the
boss (and thereby mastering the boss battle puzzle).
The feeling of this moment of mastery is very similar to what a dancer or gymnast feels
when they finally "get" a particularly difficult move or what a musician feels when
they "get" a particularly difficult riff. And, amazingly, after you master something that
required so many attempts, it sticks with you. It took me more than a month of multiple

Puzzle Examples in Action Games
Modern AAA games frequently include a number of puzzles. The following are several
different examples, but this list is certainly not comprehensive.
Sliding Blocks / Position Puzzles
Sliding block or position puzzles usually take place in third-person action games and
require the player to move large blocks around a gridded floor to create a specific pat-
tern. An alternative version of this involves positioning mirrors that are used to bounce
light or laser beams from a source to a target. One common variation is a slippery floor
that causes the blocks to move continuously until they hit a wall or other obstacle.
■ Game examples: Soul Reaver, Uncharted, Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time, Tomb
Raider, Jedi: Fallen Order, several games in the Legend of Zelda series
Physics Puzzles
Physics puzzles all involve using the physics simulation built in to the game to move
objects around the scene or hit various targets with either the player character or other
objects. This is the core mechanic in the Portal series and has become increasingly
popular as reliable physics engines like Nvidia PhysX or Havok (each built in to different
versions of Unity) have become ubiquitous in the industry. Each shot in a game of pool
(especially Nine-Ball) is also a physics puzzle.
■ Game examples: Portal, Half-Life 2, Super Mario Galaxy, Pool, Angry Birds
Chain Reaction
Chain reaction games include physics systems in which various components can inter-
act, often to create explosions or other mayhem. Players use their tools to set traps or
other series of events to either solve a puzzle or gain them an advantage over attacking
enemies. The Burnout series of racing games include a "Crash Mode" that is a puzzle
game where the player must drive their car into a specific traffic situation and cause
the greatest amount of monetary damage through a fantastic multicar collision. The
excellent co-op twin stick shooter Pixel Junk Shooter includes environmental materials
that interact with the player and each other in chain reactions (e.g., the player shoots

traption, Magicka, Red Faction: Guerilla, Just Cause 3, Bioshock, Burnout
Traversal
Traversal puzzles show you a place in the level that you need to reach but often make it

Forza: Horizon series are also traversal puzzles; the player must discover the perfect rac-

This is critically important in the "Burning Lap" puzzles of the Burnout series, which
require players to avoid making a single mistake while traversing a racecourse that

■ Game examples: Uncharted, Tomb Raider, Assassin's Creed, Oddworld: Abe's

Stealth
An extension of traversal puzzles that became important enough to merit its own genre,
stealth puzzles ask the player to traverse a level while also avoiding detection by enemy
characters, who are generally patrolling a predetermined path or following a specific
schedule. Players usually have a way to disable the enemy characters, though this can
also lead to detection if performed poorly.
■ Game examples: Metal Gear Solid, Uncharted, Oddworld: Abe's Oddysee, Mark of
the Ninja, Beyond Good and Evil, The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim, Assassin's Creed
Boss Fights
Many boss fights—especially in classic games—involve some sort of puzzle where the
player is required to learn the pattern of attacks and reactions used by a boss and to
determine a series of actions that would exploit this pattern to defeat the boss. This is
especially common in third-person action games by Nintendo like those in the Zelda,
Metroid, and Super Mario series. One element that is very common in this kind of puzzle
is the rule of three:

Dexterity and Timing
Sometimes, even after you figure out what you need to do, it still takes some time and
practice to actually achieve it. In games, this is often seen in the higher levels of rhythm
games like Osu! Tatakae! Ouendan or Dance Dance Revolution, where the actions and
timing required are clearly shown on screen, but it still takes practice to figure out the
dexterity puzzle of how to perform them, requiring several attempts before mastering
the dexterity puzzle.
A platform game example of this kind of dexterity puzzle is Oddworld: Abe's Oddysee.
When playing many levels of that game, there is first the intellectual puzzle of figuring
out how Abe should move through the level, followed by the dexterity puzzle of learn-
ing the right sequence of timing and fast hand movements on the controller to actually
make Abe move through the level that way. Similarly, in an auto racing game like Forza:
Horizon, every turn is a timing and dexterity puzzle where there is a perfect line to
take and time to brake and accelerate that are affected by the turn shape, road surface,
weather conditions, and other cars.
■ Game examples: Forza: Horizon, Oddworld: Abe's Oddysee, Dance Dance Revolution,
Osu! Tatakae! Ouendan (or its more broadly released sequel Elite Beat Agents)
Designing and Developing Puzzle
Games
When you've finished this book, and you're looking for a good first game to design and
develop yourself, a puzzle game could be a great choice for several reasons:
1. Easy to paper prototype: Nearly all puzzle games are easy to prototype and test
on paper (with the exception of action puzzle games), which means that you can do

2. Smaller scope: In general, puzzle games are smaller in scope (i.e., smaller in size
and development effort) than other kinds of digital games. This means that they can
be a great project for a team that is relatively new to developing games (though, to
be honest, any game is still a lot of work to complete).
3. Hundreds of examples: Literally hundreds, or even thousands, of puzzle games
are out there that you can look at and learn from. Any one of them could be a great
inspiration for your own puzzle game, and oftentimes, a relatively small tweak to the
design can create a wholly new game.
There are far too many excellent puzzle games for me to mention here, but some that
took relatively well-known mechanics and made them new include Angry Birds (artillery
mechanics), Candy Crush (match-three mechanics), A Good Snowman Is Hard to Build
(Sokoban mechanics), Lara Croft Go (Daleks mechanics), and my game Ledbetter

Summary
As you've seen in this chapter, puzzles are an important aspect of many games that have
single-player or multiplayer co-op modes. Puzzle design is not a large departure from
the skills you've already learned as a game designer, but some subtle differences exist.
When you design a game, the most important aspect is the moment-to-moment game-
play, whereas in puzzle design, the solution and the moment of insight are of primary
importance. (In an action puzzle such as Tetris, however, insight and solution happen
with the drop and placement of every piece.) In addition, when the player solves a tra-
ditional puzzle, being able to tell with certainty that they have found the right answers
is important; but in games, interesting decisions rely on uncertainty in the player's mind
about the outcome or correctness of decisions.
Regardless of the differences between designing puzzles and games, the iterative
design process is as critical for puzzles as it is for all other kinds of interactive experi-
ences. As a puzzle designer, you want to make prototypes and playtest just as you

The Manifesto for Agile Software
Development
For many years, a large number of software titles—including games—tended to be
developed using what is commonly known as the waterfall method of development.
Using the waterfall method, a small preproduction team would define the entire
project via a massive game design document that the production team was expected
to follow exactly as they developed the game. Using this waterfall approach often
led to games that were not tested until they neared completion, and members of these
production teams could feel more like cogs in a massive machine than actual game
developers.
With the experience you've now gained through paper and digital prototyping in this
book, I'm sure you can immediately see some issues with this approach. In 2001, the
developers who formed the Agile Alliance saw these issues as well, leading to their
Manifesto for Agile Software Development,
1
which reads as follows:
We are uncovering better ways of developing software by doing it and helping
others do it. Through this work we have come to value:
■ Individuals and interactions over processes and tools
■ Working software over comprehensive documentation
■ Customer collaboration over contract negotiation
■ Responding to change over following a plan
That is, while there is value in the items on the right, we value the items on the left
more.
Embedded in these four core values, you can see many of the principles that I've tried to
impress upon you throughout this book:
■ Following your individual design sense, continually asking questions, and
developing an understanding of procedural thinking are more important
than following predefined rules or using a specific development framework.
■ Making a simple prototype that works and iterating on it until it's fun
is more successful than waiting for months until you have the perfect game idea or
solution to your problem.
1. Kent Beck, et al. "Manifesto for Agile Software Development," Agile Alliance (2001).

■ Bouncing your ideas off of other creative people in a positive, collabora-

intellectual property.

■ Listening to and reacting to playtesters' feedback about your game is
much more important than following your original design vision. You must let your
game evolve.
Prior to my introduction of Agile development methodologies into my classes, students
often got drastically behind schedule when developing their games. In fact, they had
trouble even understanding that they were behind because they lacked the tools to
manage their development process. This also meant that playtesting student work was
difficult until very late in the project.
After my introduction of Agile and its associated tools and methodologies to my classes,
I found that several things occurred:
■ Students had a much better understanding of their progress on projects and were
better able to stick to their schedule.
■ The games being produced by students showed a marked improvement, largely
because the students' focus on constantly having a playable build allowed them to
playtest the games earlier and more frequently.
■ Student understanding of both C# and Unity increased as did their confidence in
their technical skills.
Of those three points, the first two were expected. The third initially took me by
surprise, but I have found it to be the case in every class that I have taught using Agile
methodologies. As a result, I have continued to use Agile in all of my classes, in my own
personal game development practice, and even while writing this book. I hope that you
will, too.
Scrum Methodology
In the years since 2001, many people have developed tools and methodologies to help
teams easily adapt to the Agile mentality. One of my favorites is Scrum.
Scrum actually started several years before the Agile Manifesto and was developed
by various people, but its relationship to Agile was solidified in the 2001 book Agile

making something is more important than arguing over who should own what percentage of

The Scrum Team
A Scrum team for game prototyping is composed of one Product Owner, one Scrum
Master, and an interdisciplinary Development Team consisting of up to ten other people
who are skilled in various fields, including programming, game design, modeling,
texturing, audio, etc.
■ Product Owner: The voice of the client or the voice of the future players of your
game.
4
The Product Owner wants to make sure that all the cool features make it into
the game, and they are responsible for understanding the gestalt vision of the game.
■ Scrum Master: The voice of reason. The Scrum Master runs the Daily Scrum
meeting and wants to make sure that everyone is on-task without being overworked.
The Scrum Master acts as a foil for the Product Owner by keeping a realistic eye
on how much work remains on the project and how quickly the members of the
development team are completing the tasks assigned to them. If the project is
behind schedule or certain features need to be cut, the Scrum Master is responsible
for getting the schedule back on track and ensuring any required changes happen.
■ Development Team: The people in the trenches. The development team is
composed of everyone working on the project and can include the Product Owner
and Scrum Master, who often work as standard members of the team outside of the
Daily Scrum. Individuals in the development team are assigned tasks at the Daily
Scrum and are relied upon to accomplish those tasks by the next Daily Scrum. In
Scrum, individual team members are given far more agency than in other develop-
ment methods, but that agency comes coupled with the accountability of daily
check-ins with the rest of the team.

NJ: Prentice Hall, 2002).
4. Though on rare occasions, the Product Owner is the actual client, more often it is someone
internal to the company who acts as an advocate for the client.

Product Backlog / Task List
A Scrum project starts with a product backlog (also known as a task list), which is a list
of all the features, mechanics, art, and so on that the team expects to implement for
the final game. Some of these start out pretty vague and are broken down into more
specific sub-features as development progresses.
In traditional Scrum, the Product Owner comes up with a list of user stories (i.e., things
that the user will experience when using the product), which the Scrum Master and team
then convert into a list of tasks for the product backlog. This can be helpful in your games

The Burndown Chart
I have found the burndown chart (BDC) to be one of the most useful tools in my game
development process and my classes. A burndown chart starts with a list of tasks to
be performed during the current sprint (the sprint backlog) and estimates of the
amount of time required to complete each task (in hours, days, weeks, and so on).
Throughout the sprint, the burndown chart tracks each team member's progress on the
goals that have been assigned to them and converts it into a chart that not only tracks
the total number of hours of work remaining on the sprint but also shows whether the
team is on track to finish the sprint on time.
The beauty of the burndown chart is that it converts a tremendous amount of data into
a simple chart that answers three critical questions:
1. Is the team on track to finish the sprint on time?
2. What tasks are assigned to each person?
3. Is everyone on the team being utilized well? (Or, is everyone pulling their weight?)
These three questions are often difficult to answer when you're working on any team,
but the burndown chart answers all of them very efficiently.
Daily Scrum Meetings
A Daily Scrum meeting (sometimes just called a Scrum or Scrum meeting) is a daily
15-minute morning stand-up meeting (literally, everyone with the ability to do so
stands throughout the meeting) that keeps the whole team on track. The Scrum Master
runs the meeting, during which each person answers three questions:
1. What did you accomplish since yesterday?
2. What do you plan to accomplish today?
3. What obstacles might get in your way?

That's it. The Scrum meeting is meant to get everyone on the same page quickly.
Questions 1 and 2 are checked against the burndown chart (BDC) to see how the project
is progressing. You want to keep the Scrum meeting as short as possible so that the
creative people on your team are spending very little of their time in full-group meet-
ings. For example, issues that arise as part of question #3 are never discussed in the
Scrum meeting. Instead, the Scrum Master finds a volunteer to help the person with the
potential obstacle and then moves on. Then, after the meeting is over, the person with
the issue and the volunteer discuss the obstacle without the rest of the team.
Through Scrum meetings, everyone on the team knows their responsibilities, what
everyone else is working on, and whom they can ask for help if they need it. Because
Scrum meetings happen every day, problems are raised and addressed as soon as they

Releases and Sprints
A product is broken down into releases and sprints. You can think of a release as a known
time when you will show the game to others (for example, a meeting with investors,
a public beta, or a formal playtest round) whereas a sprint is a step along the way to a
release. At the beginning of a sprint, a sprint backlog list is created that contains all the fea-
tures to complete by the end of the sprint. A sprint usually takes between 1 and 4 weeks,
and regardless of what you choose to work on during the sprint, you must have a playable
game (or a playable part of a game) by the end of the sprint. In fact, in the best case, from
the moment when you have your first playable prototype, you should strive to never have
a day that ends with the game in an unplayable state (though ensuring that is sometimes a
difficult task).
Some important moments in every sprint are
■ Sprint planning: The team and Product Owner agree on what user stories/features
should be included in the sprint. Then, the Scrum Master and team (or team leads
for larger teams) use that information to start a new burndown chart by entering all
the tasks needed for these user stories into the BDC's sprint backlog. The team then
sets the rank of each task (1 being highest priority), estimates how many hours the
task will take to complete, and assigns the task to a team member. This may involve
going back to the Product Owner with a more realistic list of user stories to be com-
pleted within the time of the sprint. This is also the time to make sure that you know
how much time each team member plans to commit to the project each day so that
you can assign them tasks accordingly.
■ Sprint work: This is the day-to-day work on the sprint, including Daily Scrum
meetings. The burndown chart and Scrum meetings will help all members of the
team to stay on track and know where everyone else is in their dev tasks. The teams

should focus throughout on getting the highest priority tasks to a ship-ready state.
Although the end of a task in a game development sprint might not be completely
"ship ready," completing individual tasks before getting distracted by others can
help ensure that you always have a playable build ready to show.
■ Sprint retrospective: After work on the sprint has been completed, it's time to
look back and see how things went. You can use the burndown chart to see what
kinds of tasks took more or less time than you anticipated and then make adjust-
ments to your estimates for the next sprint. The sprint retrospective is a time to
re-evaluate how things are going and make more informed decisions and estimates
as you lead into the next sprint.

ESTIMATING HOURS
One of the toughest tasks for programmers, artists, and other creative workers
is estimating the number of hours required to finish a task. Things almost always
take longer than you expect, except for that one thing that you think will take
20 hours but is then somehow completed in only 2. For now, you need to just
make the best guess that you can while following some simple estimation rules,
all based on one fact: As the size of a task increases, the accuracy of your estimate
necessarily decreases. If you're estimating:
■ In hours: stick to values of 1, 2, 4, or 8 hours.
■ In days: use 1, 2, 3, or 5 days.
■ In weeks: use 1, 2, 4, or 8 weeks.
However, if you're estimating anything in weeks for a sprint, you need to break it
down into much smaller tasks! In fact, especially when you're getting started with
burndown charts, I highly recommend breaking nearly all of your features down
into tasks that will take 8 hours or less to complete. Doing this difficult work early
on can really help you get an idea for how long something will actually take.
Also, it's important to remember that everything you do for this project should be
tracked on the burndown chart. Team meetings, time the producer takes manag-
ing the BDC, research time, and so on; all of it will take time, which means that
you need to track it on the chart for you to be able to accurately track your project
and improve your estimates in the future.
Sprint Progress
The right half of the Main worksheet is where all the tracking of progress toward the
sprint deadline occurs. The numbers throughout this section (columns H:Z) represent
the number of hours of work remaining on that task. The goal of everyone on the team
is to "burn down" each of these tasks to zero hours remaining by the end of the sprint,
and the average amount of work done by the entire team each day is known as the
burndown velocity (BDV). At the very least, every member of the team should fill out the
BDC at the end of every workday.
This section starts with column H showing the total hours required for each task (which
is copied from column E), and all the columns to the right of that (I:Z) show the team's

Adding New Tasks
Sometimes, new things will pop up that you didn't anticipate, and you'll need to add
new tasks in the middle of a sprint. This is not an excuse to break away from your plan
or to do poor planning in the first place; rather, new tasks should be added to the burn-
down chart to reflect the reality of your team members' work. For example, if you're in
the middle of an iOS project, and there is a required change to the Unity iOS API (Appli-

On Monday, in cell C8, Archon says "I need a break," in the section for Yesterday, but he

When working with teams, good communication is critical, and this worksheet can help
you achieve this. Before I added this Daily Scrum worksheet to the BDC, I had several
students approach me concerned because they didn't know where their team members
were or what they were working on. After implementing this worksheet in my classes,
the students who used it found that they were far less stressed about their projects.
Even if someone is unable to work for a day or two, it can be managed as long as the
rest of the team knows to expect it. I have my classes fill out the Daily Scrum worksheet
every day—even if they are able to have an in-person Daily Scrum meeting—because it
helps me better understand what I'm seeing in the two charts when I'm grading them.

Summary
As you begin to design and develop your own games, keeping your development pro-
cess on track can be difficult. In my years as a developer and professor, I have found that
the Agile mindset and Scrum methodology are two of the best tools for doing so. Of
course, I can't tell you for sure whether these tools will work as well for you as they have
for my students and me, but I strongly encourage you to give them a try. In the end, it
is not important whether Scrum and Agile are the perfect tools for you. The important
thing is that you find tools that do work for you and that you use them to help you stay
motivated and productive when working on your games.
In the next chapter, I'll examine the digital game industry and discuss ways in which you
can get involved. I'll also look at how to meet people at game development conferences
and what to look for in a university game program.
